title: Load Balancer: what it does (distributes traffic), types (L4 vs L7), algorithms (round-robin, least connections, IP hash), health checks, and when to use (every production system needs one).
keyPoints: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across a pool of backend servers for throughput, fault tolerance, and latency.
Layer 4 (transport) forwards by IP and port without reading the request; it is extremely fast and protocol-agnostic.
Layer 7 (application) reads HTTP path, cookies, or headers, enabling content-based routing to different service pools.
Round-robin cycles through servers equally; least-connections favours the least busy; IP hash provides session stickiness.
Health checks periodically probe each backend and remove unhealthy instances from rotation.
Keep servers stateless and store sessions in a shared cache rather than relying on sticky sessions for better failover.
Deploy load balancers as highly available pairs so the balancer itself is not a single point of failure.

s1_definition.oneliner: Spread traffic across healthy servers using an algorithm, route by connection (L4) or by request content (L7), and never send traffic to a server that failed its health check.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Load balancer** : a component that distributes incoming network traffic across a pool of backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and provide fault tolerance.
- **Layer 4 (L4)** : routes by transport-level information (IP address and port) without reading the request body; extremely fast and protocol-agnostic.
- **Layer 7 (L7)** : routes by application-level information (HTTP path, cookies, headers); enables content-based routing.
- **Health check** : a periodic probe that removes unhealthy backends from rotation until they recover.
- **Distribution algorithm** : the rule for choosing which backend gets the next request (round-robin, least-connections, IP hash).
s1_definition.analogy: When customers crowd into National Bank of India, a floor manager stands at the entrance and directs each person to an open teller so no single teller is overwhelmed while others sit idle. If a teller goes on break, the manager stops sending people there. The load balancer is that floor manager for servers: it spreads requests evenly, skips any server that is down, and makes the whole branch feel fast and reliable even when some tellers are unavailable.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across a pool of backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize latency, and survive failures, and it is a mandatory component of any production system that runs more than one server. Without it you can only scale up a single machine, which has a hard ceiling and is a single point of failure. With it you scale out across many servers and tolerate losing any one of them.

I always distinguish Layer 4 from Layer 7. A Layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer and forwards based on IP and port without reading the request, which is extremely fast and protocol-agnostic. A Layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request and can route by URL path, cookies, or headers, which at National Bank of India let me send heavy statement downloads to one server pool and light transfer requests to another.

The distribution algorithm decides which backend gets the next request. Round-robin cycles through servers and is fair when they are equal; least-connections sends to the least busy server and is better when request durations vary; IP hash maps each client consistently to one server for stickiness. The algorithm fixed a real problem for us on salary day, when one server was getting most of the transfer traffic while others sat idle.

The piece that makes a load balancer trustworthy is health checks. The balancer periodically probes each backend's health endpoint and removes any server that fails from rotation until it recovers, so clients never hit a dead server. The senior nuance I always add is to keep the servers stateless and store session data in a shared cache rather than relying on sticky sessions, and to deploy the balancer itself as a highly available pair so it does not become a new single point of failure.

Remember one sentence: a load balancer distributes traffic across healthy servers using algorithms like round-robin or least-connections, with health checks removing failed instances, and must itself be highly available.
